captureGuide.title: Capture Guide
captureGuide.intro: A good photo is the single biggest factor in how accurate your simulation looks. This takes two minutes and is worth doing properly.
captureGuide.footer: If a photo is rejected, it is almost always lighting or angle, not you. Retake rather than force it through.

angles.title: Take three photos
angles.why: The simulator combines them to understand your nose in three dimensions. One photo alone limits what it can show.

front.name: Front
front.detail: Looking straight at the lens, both ears equally visible, head not tilted.

left.name: Left profile
left.detail: Turn a full 90 degrees so the far eye and eyebrow disappear behind your nose.

right.name: Right profile
right.detail: The same on the other side. Both profiles matter: noses are rarely symmetrical.

lighting.title: Lighting
lighting.why: Shadows across the nose read as shape. Harsh or uneven light can make a straight bridge look curved.
tips: Face a window in daylight, or stand facing an evenly lit wall.
Use soft, indirect light; an overcast day is close to ideal.
Keep the light in front of you, level with your face.
lighting.avoid: Overhead spotlights, direct sun, a bright window behind you, or mixing warm indoor bulbs with daylight.

camera.title: Camera position and lens
camera.why: A phone's front camera is wide-angle: it enlarges whatever sits closest to it, which on a face is your nose. This distorts the measurements directly.
tips: Use the rear camera and ask someone to take the photo, or prop the phone up and use a timer.
Hold the camera at eye level, straight on, and not above or below.
Stand about an arm and a half away, then zoom slightly if you need a closer frame.
camera.avoid: Close-up selfies at arm's length. They can exaggerate nose size noticeably.

framing.title: Framing
framing.why: Detection needs enough pixels on the nose, but a cropped chin or forehead removes the reference points measurements are built on.
tips: Let your face fill roughly half to two thirds of the frame.
Include everything from above your hairline to below your chin.
Keep your head centred and upright, not tilted to one side.
On side photos, keep the lower rim of the eye socket level with the top of the ear opening (the Frankfort line). The camera shows it as a dashed line.
framing.avoid: Cropping the top of the head or the chin out of the frame.

background.title: Background
background.why: A busy background makes it harder to find the edge of your face, especially around the hair and jawline.
tips: Stand in front of a plain wall.
Pick a background that contrasts with your hair and skin.
Leave a little space behind you rather than pressing against the wall.
background.avoid: Patterned wallpaper, mirrors, or other people in the shot.

expression.title: Expression
expression.why: Smiling lifts the upper lip and rotates the base of the nose, which shifts the nasolabial angle by several degrees: one of the measurements shown here.
tips: Keep a relaxed, neutral expression.
Lips together, jaw unclenched.
Eyes open and looking at the lens.
expression.avoid: Smiling, raising your eyebrows, or holding a deliberate pose.

hair.title: Hair and glasses
hair.why: Anything covering the brow, cheek or jaw hides landmarks the simulator uses to place its measurements.
tips: Tie or clip hair back so the full face is visible.
Leave both ears uncovered.
Remove glasses: frames sit directly over the bridge of the nose.
hair.avoid: A fringe over the eyebrows, or hair falling across one cheek.

quality.title: Image quality
quality.why: Beauty filters smooth and reshape faces before the app ever sees the photo, and it cannot detect that it has happened.
tips: Turn off beauty mode, skin smoothing and any filters.
Send the original file rather than a screenshot or a messaging-app copy.
Check the photo is sharp and in focus before uploading.
quality.avoid: Screenshots, heavily compressed images, and anything already edited or retouched.

aiExplainer.title: About AI suggestions
aiExplainer.howItWorksBody: Rule-based analysis of nasal measurements from your photo (nasofrontal angle, Goode's ratio, alar width, etc.) against ethnicity- and gender-adjusted aesthetic ranges. Not a trained ML model.
aiExplainer.confidenceBody: How far the measured value is from the internal target: not a prediction of surgical outcome quality.
aiExplainer.worksBestBody: Frontal photos, even lighting, visible landmarks, first-time aesthetic changes.
aiExplainer.lessReliableBody: True profile photos, mixed-ancestry faces, revision cases, asymmetric noses, unusual lighting.
aiExplainer.footer: Use suggestions as a starting point for patient conversation, not a surgical plan. Clinical judgment always takes precedence.

howItWorks.title: How this works
howItWorks.bridgeBody: Two sliders shape the bridge. {size} makes the whole nose smaller or larger, and {width} makes the bridge narrower or wider. The highlighted area is the part of your nose they move.
howItWorks.tipBody: Three sliders shape the tip. {tip} makes it more refined or more natural, {angle} rotates it down or up, and {project} pulls it back or pushes it forward.
howItWorks.nostrilsBody: {nostrils} narrows or widens the base of your nose, at the highlighted area.
howItWorks.compareBody: There are three ways to check the result. {compare} flips between your original photo and the simulation. {slider} drags a divider between the two. {changeMap} paints the areas that actually moved, so a subtle result is still easy to see.
howItWorks.historyBody: {undo} and {redo} are in the top bar, next to the save button. {reset}, inside {more}, returns every slider to zero and restores your original photo.

critical.title: Important safety information
critical.mortalityBody: BBL has the highest mortality rate of any cosmetic procedure, primarily from fat embolism when fat is injected too deep or in excessive volume. Only proceed with a board-certified plastic surgeon experienced in safe injection technique.
critical.volumeCapBody: Estimated fat graft volume exceeds the conservative safe ceiling of 550cc per buttock. Larger volumes raise the risk of overcorrection and fat embolism; discuss a staged, more conservative plan with a board-certified surgeon.

friendlyWarnings.volumeHigh: This volume is on the higher end: larger fat grafts carry more risk and a longer recovery.
friendlyWarnings.projectionHigh: This projection may look dramatic in the preview: fat graft survival is typically 60–70%, so final results tend to be softer than shown.
friendlyWarnings.asymmetry: This preview shows some asymmetry between sides; your surgeon can discuss options to balance results.
friendlyWarnings.overcorrect: This level of change may look overcorrected; a more moderate adjustment often looks more natural.
friendlyWarnings.conservative: A more conservative approach may achieve a similar look with less risk.
friendlyWarnings.generic: Discuss this combination of changes with a board-certified surgeon before deciding.

volumeWarning.soft: Preview may slightly over-represent final volume. Fat graft survival is typically 60-70%. Results will be close but may be subtler than shown.
volumeWarning.hard: Preview volume may exceed realistic graft yield. Fat graft survival is 60–70%; final results will be more moderate. Try reducing volume or increasing waist sculpting.
volumeWarning.standaloneVolume: Maximum volume without waist sculpting may look disproportionate: fat harvesting from donor sites is not shown in this preview.

skinCapture.title: Taking a skin photo
skinCapture.intro: Light, filters and angle can hide texture and tone, or add some that is not there. A minute here makes the preview more faithful.

view.title: One front-facing photo
view.why: The estimate and the preview read both cheeks, the forehead and the chin evenly only when the face is square to the camera.
tips: Face the camera straight on, with the lens at eye level.
Hold the phone about an arm's length away, or ask someone to take it.
view.avoid: Side or three-quarter views, and photos taken from above or below.

light.title: Even, soft light from in front
light.why: Shadows and glare read as texture and colour, which is exactly what a peel changes.
tips: Face a window in daylight, or an evenly lit wall.
Keep the light level with your face.
light.avoid: Flash, harsh light from one side, or a bright window or lamp behind you.

bare.title: Bare skin, no filters
bare.why: Makeup, beauty filters and smoothing modes hide the texture and tone the preview works on.
tips: Remove makeup and products that add shine.
Turn off beauty, portrait and face-smoothing camera modes.

clear.title: Hair back, glasses off, face relaxed
clear.why: Hair and frames cover skin, and an expression folds it into lines that are not there at rest.
tips: Pull hair off the forehead and take glasses off.
Keep a neutral expression with your mouth closed.

repeat.title: Retake the same way to compare
repeat.why: A later photo only compares fairly with this one if it is taken the same way.
tips: Use the same place, the same light and the same distance each time.
repeat.avoid: Changing room, time of day or camera between photos.

problem.pain3Desc: When patients can't see the plan, dissatisfaction and revision surgeries increase; costly for both clinic and patient.

patientPrivacy.q: How does Faceify protect patient privacy?
patientPrivacy.a: All photos process in the patient's browser. No image leaves the device for the base simulator. All AI inference runs directly on the device's own hardware.

hipaaCompat.a: The browser-native architecture means Faceify does not receive, store, or transmit Protected Health Information from the base simulator. US clinics can use Faceify alongside their existing PHI workflows. BAAs are available on the Enterprise plan upon request. See /trust for the architecture statement.

gdprPdpaPipa.q: What about GDPR, PDPA, and PIPA?
gdprPdpaPipa.a: Image data does not leave the patient's device, so EU, Singapore/Thailand, and Korea/Japan data-residency rules apply at the device level, not the cloud level. DPIA available on request via partners@faceifylabs.com. The optional photoreal preview path uses Replicate (US) and is consent-gated; see /trust.

consentCapture.a: Consent is captured in the simulator UI before any procedure preview runs. The clinic owns the consent log via its own EHR. Faceify does not store consent records.

trainingTime.a: About 15 minutes for a surgeon to run their first consult. The interface is designed for in-room use, not classroom training.

OurStory.heroSubtitle: The aesthetic medicine industry generates over $70B a year. Yet the consultation (the moment that builds trust between surgeon and patient) still relies on hand-waving, stock photos, and hope.
OurStory.problemP1: Patients walk into clinics with a vague idea of what they want. Surgeons have the skill to deliver extraordinary results. But there is no shared language between the two: no way to say “this is what we are going to achieve” and <show>show it</show> in real time.
OurStory.problemP2: That gap kills conversions. It creates expectation mismatches. It leads to revision surgeries, negative reviews, and burnt-out practitioners who do brilliant work but can’t communicate it.
OurStory.problemP3: We built Faceify Labs to close that gap, permanently.
OurStory.belief1Body: A 10-second simulation closes more consultations than a 30-minute explanation. When patients can see a visualization on their own face, trust is immediate.
OurStory.belief2Body: Every simulation runs entirely in the browser. No patient image ever touches a server. Zero cloud processing, zero data risk, zero compliance headaches.
OurStory.belief3Body: Surgeons have 8 minutes per consultation. If a tool takes longer to set up than the conversation itself, it won’t be used. Our engine renders in under 200ms.
OurStory.belief4Body: Our 468-point facial mesh is tested across Asian, South Asian, Middle Eastern, African, and European facial phenotypes. We evaluate landmark accuracy across ethnicities, not just Western benchmark sets.
OurStory.builtP1: Faceify Labs is a real-time surgical simulation engine. Upload a patient photo, and our 468-point face mesh maps every anatomical landmark: nasal bridge angle, alar base width, malar projection, orbital aperture, jawline contour.
OurStory.builtP2: Then adjust. Rhinoplasty tip rotation, dorsal hump reduction, Botox zone smoothing, filler volume projection, chemical peel texture refinement, blepharoplasty lid reshaping: all rendered in real time, all running on the device in front of you.
OurStory.builtP3: No downloads. No GPU servers. No per-image billing. Just open a browser, upload a photo, and show the patient a visualization to explore.
OurStory.differentP1: Most simulation tools are built by graphics companies who treat the face like a game asset. Stretch here, blur there, ship it. The result looks impressive in a demo and absurd in a consultation room.
OurStory.differentP2: We built ours with anatomical constraints. Every deformation respects tissue mechanics. You can’t project a nasal tip beyond what cartilage allows, can’t inflate cheeks past the malar boundary, can’t smooth skin without accounting for Fitzpatrick type and Glogau classification.
OurStory.whyFaceDesc: , because this is a face-first platform. Every algorithm, every UI decision, every data model is optimized for facial anatomy.
OurStory.whyIfyDesc: , because we turn complexity into action. Simplify. Clarify. Quantify. We take the most complex surface in the human body and make it legible to both the surgeon and the patient.
OurStory.whyLabsDesc: , because we are not a finished product. We’re a research-grade platform that ships production features. Every deployment teaches us something. Every clinic partnership refines the model.

hero.title: IV Therapy

iv-therapy.whatItIs: IV therapy (intravenous therapy) delivers vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, and hydration directly into your bloodstream via a small catheter, bypassing the digestive system for higher absorption rates than oral supplements. Formulas range from basic saline hydration to high-dose vitamin C, glutathione brightening drips, NAD+ longevity infusions, and immune-boosting cocktails. A typical session takes 30–60 minutes in a clinic recliner.
iv-therapy.whatToExpect: You'll complete a brief health intake form before your first session. A nurse or doctor inserts the IV line, usually in the forearm, and you relax while the drip runs. Most people feel a cooling sensation and sometimes a subtle metallic taste. Mild bruising at the insertion site is normal. High-dose vitamin C or magnesium drips occasionally cause a warm flush. Sessions run 30–90 minutes depending on the formula. You can resume normal activity immediately.
iv-therapy.whatToAskSurgeon: Ask the clinic: Which formulas are mixed on-site vs pre-packaged? Who administers the drip, a doctor, nurse, or technician? hero.title: PRP Treatments
hero.subtitle: Platelet-rich plasma for skin rejuvenation, hair restoration, and accelerated healing, using your own biology.

prp.whatItIs: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) therapy uses concentrated platelets from your own blood to stimulate collagen production, accelerate healing, and promote hair follicle activity. A small blood draw is centrifuged to separate the plasma, which is then micro-needled or injected into the treatment area. Applications include facial rejuvenation (the "vampire facial") and hair thinning.
prp.whatToExpect: A blood draw of around 15–30 ml is taken, spun in a centrifuge for 10–15 minutes, and then the PRP is applied or injected. Facial PRP involves micro-needling across the treatment area. Expect redness and mild swelling for 24–48 hours. Scalp PRP involves a grid of small injections; tenderness and minor swelling are normal for 1–2 days. Changes typically develop over 3–6 months, often across about 3 sessions. Your provider will advise on a plan.
prp.whatToAskSurgeon: Ask the clinic: What concentration of platelets does your centrifuge produce? How many sessions are in the recommended protocol? Do you combine PRP with microneedling or exosomes for better results? What are realistic timelines for seeing improvement? Are there any contraindications (blood thinners, auto-immune conditions)?

mesotherapy.whatItIs: Mesotherapy delivers a customised cocktail of vitamins, minerals, enzymes, hyaluronic acid, and pharmaceutical compounds via a series of superficial micro-injections into the mesoderm (middle skin layer). It is used for skin hydration (skin boosters), reducing localised fat deposits, cellulite reduction, scalp hair loss, and brightening dull skin. The injection solution is tailored to your specific concern by the treating physician.
mesotherapy.whatToExpect: Multiple tiny injections are administered across the treatment zone using a very fine needle or mesotherapy gun. Sessions take 20–45 minutes. Expect mild redness, micro-bumps, and light bruising for 24–72 hours. Numbing cream is applied beforehand. For fat-reduction mesotherapy (Aqualyx or similar), localised swelling and firmness for several days is normal. Most protocols require 4–8 sessions spaced 1–2 weeks apart.
mesotherapy.whatToAskSurgeon: Ask the clinic: What solution formulation are you using and why? Is the product CE-marked or licensed in this country? How many sessions are typically needed for my concern? What are the risks of unevenness or granuloma formation? Should I avoid exercise, sun, or alcohol before and after?

The treatment is largely painless; suction during extraction can feel slightly uncomfortable. No downtime. Sessions last 30–60 minutes. Skin appears visibly brighter and more hydrated immediately. Mild redness resolves within an hour. Monthly sessions are common for maintenance.

lipolytic-injections.shortBlurb: Fat-dissolving injections for targeted body contouring without surgery.

hero.title: Lipolytic Injections
hero.subtitle: Non-surgical fat dissolution for double chin, flanks, and body contouring, zero downtime.

lipolytic-injections.whatItIs: Lipolytic injections (also called fat-dissolving injections, Aqualyx, Kybella, or phosphatidylcholine injections) break down and destroy fat cells in targeted areas without surgery. The most common treatment areas are the submental area (double chin), flanks, inner thighs, arms, and back fat. The destroyed fat cells are eliminated via the lymphatic system over 4–8 weeks after each session.
lipolytic-injections.whatToExpect: The treatment area is cleansed and numbed. A fine needle delivers the solution in a grid pattern across the fat deposit. Significant swelling, hardness, and bruising for 3–7 days is normal: it's the inflammatory response that triggers fat cell breakdown. Multiple sessions (typically 2–6) are spaced 4–8 weeks apart. Changes typically become visible 8–12 weeks after the last session. Your provider can explain how results are maintained.
lipolytic-injections.whatToAskSurgeon: Ask the clinic: Which product are you using, Aqualyx, Kybella, or a generic phosphatidylcholine? How many vials per session for my area? What is the realistic % reduction I can expect? Am I a good candidate given my BMI and skin laxity? What happens if I gain weight after treatment? Can fat redistribute to adjacent areas?

chemical-peels.name: Chemical Peels
chemical-peels.shortBlurb: Controlled skin exfoliation with acids to improve the appearance of texture, tone, acne-prone skin, pigmentation, and ageing.

hero.title: Chemical Peels
hero.subtitle: Controlled chemical exfoliation to resurface skin, reduce pigmentation, and improve tone and texture.

chemical-peels.whatItIs: Chemical peels apply a controlled acid solution to the skin to remove damaged outer layers and stimulate collagen synthesis. Depth categories are superficial (AHA/BHA: glycolic, salicylic), medium (TCA: trichloroacetic acid), and deep (phenol). Superficial peels target the appearance of uneven tone, blemish-prone skin, and dullness with no downtime. Medium peels address deeper pigmentation, acne scarring, and fine lines with 5–7 days of peeling. Deep peels produce dramatic resurfacing with 1–2 weeks' recovery.
chemical-peels.whatToExpect: The skin is thoroughly cleansed before the peel solution is applied with a brush or gauze. Superficial peels cause a mild tingling or stinging sensation that resolves quickly; medium peels cause more pronounced stinging and are often neutralised after a set time. Expect skin to appear bronzed, then peel in sheets for 3–10 days depending on depth. Sun avoidance and SPF use are commonly advised while skin recovers. Follow your provider's guidance. A series of 3–6 superficial peels spaced 2–4 weeks apart is the standard starting protocol.
chemical-peels.whatToAskSurgeon: Ask the clinic: Which peel depth and acid type are you recommending for my concern and skin type? How many sessions are in the protocol? What pre-peel prep (retinoid priming, hydroquinone) is needed? What is the downtime and what does the peeling stage look like? What sunscreen and aftercare products do you recommend?

s01.heading: Browser-native inference. Zero server PHI.
s01.baseTitle: Base simulator: real-time landmark detection and rendering run in the browser
s01.baseBody: Facial landmark detection (468 points) and AI model inference run entirely in the browser. No image bytes are transmitted to Faceify servers during standard simulation. Model weights are fetched once (self-hosted, with CDN fallback) and run locally. Your photo leaves your device only if you turn on the optional AI photoreal preview (sent to a third-party provider) or choose to save a simulation to your account.
s01.diffusionTitle: Photoreal path: explicit disclosure of third-party transmission
s01.diffusionBody: When a user activates the photoreal preview and grants AI photo consent, the patient photo (base64 data URL) is transmitted to Replicate, a US-based GPU cloud provider, via /api/simulation/diffusion-preview. Replicate generates the preview and returns a URL. The image is not persisted to Faceify's database; it exists on Replicate's CDN for their TTL only.
s01.diffusionGeoBlock: US users are blocked at the API route level (HTTP 451). Non-US users (including UK and AU) are exposed to this third-party transmission once they grant explicit AI photo consent. The consent modal is being updated to name Replicate by name and describe the US-based transfer.

s02.heading: Regulatory frameworks: honest status
s02.intro: The architectural fact (browser-native inference, zero server PHI on the base path) is the strongest compliance asset. The diffusion path creates obligations that are not yet fully met. This table shows both.

s03.heading: Event data and sub-processor matrix
s03.replicateCalloutLabel: Replicate: patient photo transmitted (diffusion path only)
s03.replicateCallout: For non-US users who activate the photoreal preview, the patient's facial photo (base64) is transmitted to Replicate. US users are geo-blocked. Non-US users see an explicit AI photo consent modal. Replicate is a US-based company; no BAA or DPA is currently in place. This is the most significant sub-processor disclosure on this page.
s03.tableIntro: Every vendor that receives data on our behalf. Sub-processor list last reviewed 2026-05-26. We update within 7 days of any vendor change.
s03.realtimeCameraTitle: Realtime mode: camera feed stays on-device
s03.realtimeCameraBody: When Realtime mode is active, the Banuba SDK processes the camera feed entirely within the browser WASM runtime. No image frames or face landmarks are transmitted to Faceify Labs or any third party. The Banuba license token is validated locally; the SDK does not phone home.

s04.heading: How consent is captured and who owns it
s04.capturedBody: Consent is collected in-app before any procedure preview runs. The consent gate is enforced at the route level: no simulation output is returned before the patient has acknowledged the terms.
s04.ownershipBody: Consent records are owned by the clinic, not Faceify. Faceify does not store consent records. The clinic's EHR or patient management system is responsible for maintaining the consent audit trail per their local regulatory requirements.
s04.diffusionConsentLabel: Diffusion path: explicit AI photo consent
s04.diffusionConsentBody: For the photoreal preview, an explicit AI photo consent modal names Replicate, Inc. as the US-based GPU compute provider, describes the data transfer to the US, and states that the base simulator runs entirely in-browser without any data transfer. For UK users, the modal discloses the IDTA gap (no signed agreement with Replicate yet, ICO is the supervisory authority). For AU users, the modal provides the APP 8 cross-border disclosure. Consent is double opt-in; declining disables only the photoreal feature and the base simulator remains fully available.

s05.body: Security questions, BAA and DPA requests, vulnerability disclosure, and procurement questionnaires:
s05.dpia: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for the photoreal diffusion path is available upon request. Response within 5 business days.

meta.title: VR Consult Mode Setup Guide
meta.description: How to set up and use VR consult mode with your Meta Quest or Apple Vision Pro headset.

VRSetupGuide.heroSubtitle: Walk around your patient's 3D face at real-world scale, adjust procedure parameters in mid-air, and exit back to 2D with all values preserved.

s01.heading: The VR consult environment.
s01.face: A 3D model of your patient's face renders at real-world scale, 50 cm in front of you, at eye level.
s01.sliders: A floating parameter panel appears to your right. Each slider corresponds to a procedure parameter.
s01.locomotion: Walk around the face by pressing the right thumbstick forward and releasing to teleport.
s01.adjustment: Grab a slider handle with the right trigger and drag to adjust. The face deforms in real time.
s01.sync: When you exit VR, all parameter values remain set in the 2D simulator. No data is lost.

s02.heading: Supported headsets.
s02.questLine: Meta Quest 2, Quest 3, and Quest Pro via Meta Quest Browser.
s02.visionProLine: Apple Vision Pro via Safari on visionOS. Apple has not yet shipped WebXR support; availability is expected but not confirmed.
s02.otherLine: Any WebXR-capable browser. Works but is not validated by our team.
s02.steamVRLine: Desktop VR headsets requiring SteamVR. WebXR sessions are not available through SteamVR.
s02.quest1Line: Meta Quest 1. Insufficient GPU performance for real-time 3D deformation.
s02.iosLine: iOS and iPadOS Safari. WebXR is not yet supported on these platforms.

s03.heading: Getting started on Quest 2, Quest 3, or Quest Pro.
s03.step1: Put on the headset and open Meta Quest Browser. This is the browser app installed on the Quest itself, not a desktop preview or desktop Chrome.
s03.step3: Sign in with your surgeon account credentials.
s03.step4: Open a procedure simulator. For example: /surgeon/simulate/rhinoplasty or visit the simulator hub.
s03.step5: The "View in VR" button appears in the top-right corner of the simulator. Click it.
s03.step6: Grant the headset permission when the browser prompts. The VR session begins.
s03.bookmarkBody: In Meta Quest Browser, tap the menu icon and select Bookmarks, then Add Bookmark to save the simulator URL. For quicker access, you can add Faceify to the Quest Home library through Meta Quest Browser settings.
s03.visionProBody: When Apple ships WebXR support in visionOS Safari, the setup flow is identical: open Safari on visionOS, navigate to the simulator, and click the "View in VR" button. There is no additional configuration.

s04.heading: Controller reference.
s04.gesture1Desc: Teleport. Aim where you want to stand and release the thumbstick to jump there.
s04.gesture2Label: Right trigger on a slider handle
s04.gesture2Desc: Grab and drag to adjust the parameter. The face deforms as you move your hand.
s04.gesture3Desc: Dismiss the onboarding card on your first VR session. It does not appear again on the same device.

s05.heading: Troubleshooting.
s05.issue1Title: "View in VR" button does not appear
s05.issue1Body: The button only shows when navigator.xr is available. Open the simulator in Meta Quest Browser directly on the headset, not in a desktop browser or the Quest desktop preview.
s05.issue2Body: Go to Meta Quest Browser settings, find Faceify Labs under site permissions, and enable VR. Reload the page and try again.
s05.issue3Body: Close other apps running on the headset, restart Meta Quest Browser, and try again. If the crash repeats, power-cycle the headset.
s05.issue4Body: This is a known issue we are actively investigating. Please contact support and include the procedure name and headset model.
s05.issue5Body: Close background apps on the Quest. Ensure your Wi-Fi connection is on the 5 GHz band, preferably Wi-Fi 6. Move closer to the router if signal is weak.

s06.heading: Honest status.
s06.limit1Title: Realtime mode active across all 13 simulators; morphing pending effect bundles
s06.limit1Body: Realtime mode uses the Banuba SDK to track faces on a live camera feed. Tracking is active. Procedure-specific morphing is not yet applied during the live feed; the custom Banuba effect bundle is awaiting deployment. The wiring is complete and will activate once the bundle ships.
s06.limit2Title: Photoreal preview not available in VR
s06.limit2Body: The diffusion-based photoreal preview runs as a 2D panel and does not carry over into VR. View it in 2D before or after your VR session.
s06.limit3Body: VR consult mode is a Founding Partner preview. It is in active validation with our first cohort. Please share any issues with the team at partners@faceifylabs.com.

sModes.heading: Which mode to use.
sModes.intro: Faceify Labs has three simulation modes. Each is designed for a distinct point in the consultation workflow.
sModes.row2dBestFor: Initial patient consult. Async review. Share via email.
sModes.row3dBestFor: Walking around the 3D face model in VR during a surgeon-led consult.
sModes.rowRealtimeBestFor: Live in-room consult. Hold an iPad or laptop camera to the patient's face.

sRealtime.heading: Using Realtime mode.
sRealtime.requirementsBody: Any device with a front-facing camera. A laptop, iPad, or phone all work. No headset required. The Realtime tab appears in the simulator dimension toggle when the platform token is configured.
sRealtime.browserSupportBody: Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox (latest versions). Safari on iOS and iPadOS grants camera access. iPad Safari is the canonical surgeon-side device.
sRealtime.step1: Open the procedure simulator on the device with the camera. For example: /surgeon/simulate/rhinoplasty.
sRealtime.step3: Click "Grant camera access" when the browser prompts.
sRealtime.step4: Hold the device so the patient's face fills approximately 70% of the frame.
sRealtime.step5: Face tracking starts automatically. A "Tracking active" indicator appears when the face is detected.
sRealtime.step6: When the morph bundle is deployed: adjust procedure parameters via the slider panel. The morph applies live to the camera feed.
sRealtime.morphPendingBody: The Banuba custom effect bundle that binds slider values to live deformation is awaiting deployment. Tracking works now. Morphing will activate when the bundle ships. An ops task is open.
sRealtime.privacyBody: Camera feed processes entirely on-device via Banuba SDK. No image data is sent to Faceify Labs or any third party. Banuba SDK validates its license locally without phoning home.
sRealtime.ts1Body: The admin needs to add NEXT_PUBLIC_BANUBA_CLIENT_TOKEN to Vercel environment variables. Contact partners@faceifylabs.com.
sRealtime.ts2Body: Enable camera access in your browser settings and reload the page.
sRealtime.ts3Title: Face tracking shows "Initialising" and does not progress
sRealtime.ts3Body: Reload the page. If the issue persists, switch back to 2D mode and contact support.
sRealtime.ts4Title: Slider moves but morph does not apply
sRealtime.ts4Body: The Banuba effect bundle has not yet been deployed. This is a known ops task. Return to 2D mode for parameter preview.

AcneAnalyser.reportPigmentBody1: Active acne often looks red. After a spot heals it can leave a flat brown or dark mark, called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH). Acne lesions tend to improve weeks before PIH fades.
AcneAnalyser.reportPigmentBody2: In a study of 324 people who consulted a dermatologist for acne in seven Asian countries, 58.2% had PIH, and many found it as bothersome as the acne itself, or more so.

AcneAnalyser.reportTreatmentIntro: The American Academy of Dermatology's 2024 guideline makes 18 evidence-based recommendations and 5 good practice statements. It is written for clinicians. This summary does not choose a treatment for you; it shows the options a dermatologist will weigh.
AcneAnalyser.reportLadderStrongItems: Benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline.
AcneAnalyser.reportLadderIsoItems: Oral isotretinoin, for acne that is severe, causes psychosocial burden or scarring, or has not responded to standard oral or topical treatment.
AcneAnalyser.reportLadderConditionalItems: Topical clascoterone, salicylic acid and azelaic acid; oral minocycline and sarecycline; combined oral contraceptive pills; spironolactone.
AcneAnalyser.reportLadderGoodPracticeItems: Combining topical treatments that work in different ways, limiting oral antibiotics and pairing them with topical treatment, and steroid injections for larger lesions.
AcneAnalyser.reportLadderNote: Strong and conditional describe how firm the evidence is, not how strong the treatment is. The published summary does not sort these options by severity, so neither does this report.

AcneAnalyser.reportMethodMeasuredBody: The forehead and both cheeks were located with face landmarks. Brows and hair were masked out, and each zone was scored from 0 to 100 by how much redder its spots are than the skin around them. The overall score weights each cheek slightly more than the forehead.
AcneAnalyser.reportMethodLabelsBody: An image model reads close crops of the inflamed spots it finds and names the closest of five types: blackheads, whiteheads, papules, pustules or cysts. A type is shown only on zones at Mild or above, and only when the closest match is clear.
AcneAnalyser.reportMethodPhotoBody: A photo cannot feel depth, so it cannot confirm nodules or cysts, and it is weakest at small, non-inflamed lesions. This report covers the face only, not the chest or back. Lighting, makeup and camera processing all change what the image shows.
AcneAnalyser.reportMethodGradeBody: There is no universally accepted acne grading scale. Clinical scales such as IGA, GAGS and the Hayashi criteria are scored by a trained clinician examining the skin, and some include the chest and back. This report does not assign any of them.
AcneAnalyser.reportMethodPrivacyBody: The analysis ran in your browser and the photo was not uploaded. If you save this scan to your history, a small thumbnail and these results are stored in your account.

AcneAnalyser.typeInfoBlackheads: Open comedones: pores clogged with oil and dead skin cells that oxidise and turn dark. Common on the nose and forehead. Salicylic acid and retinoids help.
AcneAnalyser.typeInfoWhiteheads: Closed comedones: clogged pores covered by a thin layer of skin. Appear as small white/flesh-coloured bumps. Salicylic acid and gentle exfoliation help.
AcneAnalyser.typeInfoPapules: Small, red, inflamed bumps without visible pus. Caused by inflammation in blocked pores. Benzoyl peroxide and niacinamide can help reduce redness.
AcneAnalyser.typeInfoPustules: Inflamed lesions with a visible white/yellow centre, what people commonly call pimples. Avoid squeezing: it can cause scarring. Benzoyl peroxide spot treatment helps.
AcneAnalyser.typeInfoCyst: Deep, painful, pus-filled lesions beneath the skin. The most severe form of acne with the highest scarring risk. A dermatologist should evaluate cystic acne: OTC treatments are often insufficient.
AcneAnalyser.levelInfoClear: No significant acne signals detected. Maintain your current skincare routine and sun protection.
AcneAnalyser.levelInfoMild: Low-level acne activity, mostly a few blackheads/whiteheads or minor redness. OTC treatments are typically effective at this stage.
AcneAnalyser.levelInfoModerate: Noticeable acne with a mix of comedones and inflamed lesions across multiple zones. A consistent OTC routine can help. Consider a dermatologist if no improvement after 8 weeks.
AcneAnalyser.levelInfoSevere: Widespread inflamed lesions and/or deep cysts across multiple zones. Professional evaluation is recommended: prescription treatments may be more effective than OTC alone.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoForehead: The T-zone area is rich in oil glands, making it prone to blackheads and whiteheads. Often linked to hair products or friction from hats and headwear.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoLeftCheek: Cheek acne is commonly linked to phone contact, pillowcases, and face-touching. Can also be hormonal or product-related.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoRightCheek: Cheek acne is commonly linked to phone contact, pillowcases, and face-touching. Can also be hormonal or product-related.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoNose: The nose has the highest density of oil glands on the face: comedones (blackheads) are very common here. Avoid pore strips which can damage skin.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoChin: Chin acne is strongly linked to hormonal fluctuations. Common before the menstrual period. Responds well to consistent salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide.
AcneAnalyser.zoneInfoJaw: Jawline acne is typically hormonal, common in adult women. Often presents as deeper, cystic lesions. A dermatologist can help with hormonal acne that does not respond to OTC treatments.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipComedonal: Avoid heavy, oil-based products and makeup; they can clog pores and worsen blackheads and whiteheads.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipInflammatory: Do not pick, squeeze, or pop lesions; this spreads bacteria, worsens inflammation, and increases scarring risk.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipPIH: Post-acne dark marks (PIH) can take 3–12 months to fade. Consistent sun protection is the single most effective way to speed fading. Ingredients like niacinamide, azelaic acid, and vitamin C can help.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipIntroduce: Introduce new active ingredients one at a time, waiting 2–3 weeks before adding another. This helps identify what works and prevents irritation.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipPatience: Be patient: most OTC acne treatments take 4–8 weeks to show visible improvement. Consistency matters more than intensity.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipDermatologist: If acne is painful, widespread, or not improving after 8 weeks of OTC treatment, consult a dermatologist. Prescription treatments can be more effective with fewer side effects under professional supervision.
AcneAnalyser.skincareTipPillowcase: Change pillowcases 2–3 times per week and avoid touching your face throughout the day.

about.heading: What rhinoplasty is.
about.body: Rhinoplasty reshapes the nose: the bridge, the tip, the nostrils, or all of them. In a closed rhinoplasty the cuts are inside the nostrils. An open rhinoplasty adds a small cut between them, which gives the surgeon a clearer view of the cartilage. If the septum is crooked, it can be straightened in the same operation to help breathing.

measure.caveat: References are textbook norms, drawn mostly from Caucasian populations. Use them as reference points for discussion, not as targets for every patient.

s2.title: Turn on the overlays

evidence.heading: What rhinoplasty imaging studies found.
evidence.subtext: These studies used other imaging tools, not Faceify.

punthakee.body: of 112 rhinoplasty patients rated the side-view simulation very close to or identical with their result. For the front view, 41.1%.

agarwal.body: of 300 ratings by 12 blinded surgeons judged the simulation a realistic picture of the result, fully or with room to be closer. In 32% it was not.

result.q: Does the simulation show the surgical result?
result.a: No. It shows a proposed change on the patient's photo so you can agree on direction and degree. It does not model healing, skin thickness or cartilage.

photos.a: A well-lit front photo and a true side profile. Side-view measurements such as the nasolabial and nasofrontal angles need the profile.

references.q: Do the reference ranges apply to every patient?
references.a: No. They are textbook norms, drawn mostly from Caucasian populations. Use them as reference points for discussion, not as targets.

camera.q: Can I use a live camera?
camera.a: Yes, for rhinoplasty. Live camera mode shows the change on the patient's face in real time, and the camera frame is processed on the device.

cases.heading: Common nose shapes, each set in the simulator.
cases.subtext: Each case is a different AI-generated face. The after is the simulator's own output, captioned with the controls that made it.
cases.caption: <changes></changes> on an AI-generated face. Simulator output, illustrative only.

dorsalHump.name: Dorsal hump
dorsalHump.body: A bump on the bridge, plainest in profile. Dorsal height lowers it and leaves the tip as it is.

bulbousTip.name: Bulbous tip
bulbousTip.body: A broad, rounded tip with little definition. Tip width narrows the lobule and leaves the bridge as it is.

wideNostrils.name: Wide nostrils
wideNostrils.body: Nostrils that flare wide at the base. Alar base width brings the base in and leaves the tip as it is.

droopingTip.name: Drooping tip
droopingTip.body: A tip that hangs below the line of the bridge, often with age. Tip rotation turns it up and shows more of the columella.

recovery.heading: Recovery, week by week.
recovery.subtext: What most people go through after a first rhinoplasty.
recovery.note: Typical timings from the NHS, ASPS, BAPRAS, Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus. Your surgeon's plan comes first.

splint.title: Splint off
splint.body: The splint and stitches come off at about a week, sometimes two. Any packing inside the nose is out within a few days.

work.title: Back to work or school
work.body: Most people are back at a desk or in class within one to two weeks.

bruising.title: Bruising fades
bruising.body: Bruising and redness around the eyes and nose fade over two to three weeks.

exercise.title: Exercise again
exercise.body: Walking is fine within days. Strenuous exercise and contact sports wait four to six weeks. Keep glasses off the bridge until your surgeon says otherwise.

swelling.title: Swelling settles
swelling.body: Most of the swelling is gone within a few months. The tip is the last part to settle.

final.title: The final shape
final.body: The refined result, especially at the tip, is judged at about a year.

cost.heading: What a first rhinoplasty typically costs.
cost.subtext: Typical ranges for a first rhinoplasty. Revision and rib-cartilage work cost more. Your quote depends on the surgeon, the technique and what the fee includes.
cost.source: Compiled from clinic price lists and medical travel sites published in 2025 and 2026. A guide only, not a quote.

prepare.heading: Bring the picture, and your questions.

s1.title: Try the change on your photo
s1.body: Move one part at a time until it looks right to you, then save the before and after to show your surgeon.

s2.title: Check the surgeon
s2.body: Ask about their training, how many rhinoplasties they do, and to see their own before and after photos.

s3.title: Ask what is realistic
s3.body: Show the picture and ask what your skin, cartilage and breathing allow. The simulation is a starting point, not a promise.

s4.title: Ask about the plan
s4.body: Open or closed, what the fee includes, where you recover, and when you come back for checks.

simulation.q: Will my nose look exactly like the simulation?
simulation.a: No. It shows a proposed change on your photo so you and your surgeon can agree on direction and degree. It does not model healing, skin thickness or cartilage.

pain.a: Most people describe soreness and a blocked nose rather than severe pain. Ordinary pain relief usually covers it, and it eases within a few days to a week.

permanent.a: Largely, yes. The change is long-lasting, though your nose keeps ageing with the rest of your face.

breathing.a: Often. If the wall between the nostrils, the septum, is crooked, it can be straightened in the same operation. This is called a septorhinoplasty.

age.q: How old do I need to be?
age.a: Old enough that your nose has finished growing. Many surgeons wait until about 15 to 16 for girls and a little later for boys.

risks.a: Bleeding, infection, a numb nose, trouble breathing, a changed sense of smell, and a result you are not happy with, which sometimes means a second operation. A hole in the septum is a rare risk.

limits.heading: What a photo can and cannot see.
limits.subtext: What the analyser does not see, with the studies behind the limits that have one.
limits.disclaimer: The Acne Analyser is for cosmetic awareness. It is not a diagnosis and does not replace an examination by a dermatologist. If your acne is painful, leaving scars or getting worse, see one.

comedones.title: Blackheads and whiteheads are not red.
comedones.body: The analyser reads redness, so a face with only blackheads and whiteheads can read Clear. Photographs miss small, non-inflamed spots in general. These types are matched only from a close-up photo of a single spot.

zones.title: Nose, chin and jaw are not scored.
zones.body: Stubble, lips and nostrils read as redness there, so this version leaves those zones out. Acne along the jawline does not change your result.

marks.title: Dark marks are not measured.
marks.body: The marks old spots leave behind are not scored. Even dermatologists disagree on whether a mark is redness or a dark mark, most of all when active acne is present.

darkerSkin.title: Darker skin can read lower.
darkerSkin.body: Redness shows less contrast on darker skin, so the same acne can score a level lower. Research on software that grades acne from photos is also narrow: a 2025 review found most studies used photos of only a few ethnic groups. Read a low result on darker skin with extra caution.

depth.title: A photo cannot feel depth.
depth.body: Nodules and cysts are judged partly by touch and depth, which no camera can supply. Treat a cyst match as a reason to see a dermatologist, not as a finding.

notDermatologist.title: Software is not a dermatologist.
notDermatologist.body: The Acne Analyser has not been through a clinical study, so it makes no claim about how often it agrees with one. A dermatologist's examination remains the standard.

diagnosis.a: No. The Acne Analyser is a cosmetic awareness tool. It describes what your photo shows, zone by zone, and points to the kinds of care the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline describes. It does not diagnose acne or any other condition, and it does not replace a dermatologist.

upload.a: The analysis runs in your browser, so your photo is not uploaded to be analysed. If you choose to save a scan to your history, a small thumbnail and your result are stored in your account so your history can show them. Your full-size photo is not part of a saved scan.

photo.a: Face a window for even, natural light. Use clean, bare skin with no makeup or tinted sunscreen, pull your hair back, and hold the phone straight on so your whole face, forehead to chin, is in frame. Turn off beauty filters. JPEG, PNG and WebP photos all work.

includes.a: Every analysis shows your overall level and score. The full report adds the zone map on your photo, a score for your forehead and each cheek, the closest-match lesion type where inflamed spots are found, a treatment ladder set out against the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline, a morning and evening routine, a printable report, a summary for your dermatologist and your scan history.

types.q: How does it name lesion types?
types.a: Only where a zone shows redness. An image model looks at close crops of the inflamed spots the analyser finds and names the closest of five types: blackheads, whiteheads, papules, pustules or cysts. Clear skin never gets a type. It is a closest match, not a diagnosis. Blackheads and whiteheads are not red, so they are matched only from a close-up photo of a single spot.

zones.q: Why are the nose, chin and jaw not scored?
zones.a: In those zones, stubble, lips and nostrils look like redness to a camera, and the scores they produced were misleading. So this version scores your forehead and both cheeks, and shows the nose, chin and jaw as not scored. Acne along the jawline does not change your result, so mention it to your dermatologist.

skinTones.q: Does it work on my skin tone?
skinTones.a: It runs on every skin tone, but redness, which is what it measures, shows less contrast on darker skin, so the same acne can read a level lower. Your skin type is never guessed from your photo: you can answer one optional question about how your skin reacts to sun, and your routine adds care against dark marks. On darker skin, read a low result with extra caution.

dermatologist.q: Can I share it with my dermatologist?
dermatologist.a: Yes. The full report includes a printable report and a short plain-text summary in a dermatologist's terms, which you can paste into a message or bring to an appointment. It is a starting point for that conversation, not a substitute for the examination.

access.a: One payment opens the full report for 24 hours. Every analysis you run in that window shows the full report, and the scans you save stay in your account. There is no subscription and nothing renews.
